title: Jivaka the physician
hookLine: the court doctor who treated the Buddha and the monks for free

lines: A BABY ON A RUBBISH HEAP.
cards: Is it alive? That question comes near the start of the Vinaya's account of the doctor.

A newborn has been left on a rubbish heap in Rajagaha, with crows gathering around it, and a prince named Abhaya, passing by early in the morning, stops and asks. Yes, his people tell him, it's alive.
So the prince has the baby carried home and raised. The boy's name, the text says, came from that answer: Jivaka, the one who lives. Today, the doctor that child grew up to be.

teach.b: First, the test. Grown, Jivaka goes away to study medicine with a well-known teacher. The Vinaya tells of his final exam: take a spade, walk all around the town, and bring back any plant that is not medicine.
Jivaka comes back with nothing. Every plant he found, he says, could heal something. His teacher sends him home: you've learned enough to make a living.
Back in Rajagaha he cures King Bimbisara, and the king appoints him physician to the king himself, to his household, and to the Buddha and the monks.
Third, the Buddha's doctor. When the Buddha's body is out of balance, Jivaka treats him gently, the text says, with a remedy breathed in from lotus flowers.
He cares for the monks so freely that, the Vinaya says, some sick men began asking to be ordained just to be treated by him.
So Jivaka asked the Buddha not to ordain people with certain diseases, and the Buddha made that a rule. Fourth, the gifts.

Jivaka gives the Buddha a pair of fine robes, and from then on monks may accept robes from householders. He has a mango grove near Rajagaha, where the Jivaka Sutta is set; tradition says he gave it to the sangha.
The baby left on a rubbish heap becomes the man who's there when the body breaks down. And his first lesson was a field with no useless plants in it.

how: Jivaka is honored in some Buddhist communities as a patron of healers; in Thailand, some traditional massage and medicine schools pay respect to him before lessons, and monasteries still receive medicine as one of the requisites lay people offer.

games.q: you're the young student. your teacher says: walk all around the town and bring back any plant that is not medicine. you search everywhere. what do you bring back?
o: the most useless weed you can find.
nothing: every plant could heal something.
a basket of the best herbs, to impress him.
games.why: he comes back empty-handed, and that's how the teacher knows he's ready.

practice: Think of one person whose body is having a hard time, a parent with a bad knee, a friend just home from the hospital, or your own tired self. Ask Jivaka's question from the test: what's near at hand that could help?
A glass of water, a walk together, a bedtime kept: let one simple answer come.

wordCard.voice: Jivaka. The one who lives: found as a baby on a rubbish heap, he became doctor to a king, to the Buddha and to the monks. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Jivaka: the one who lives; the Vinaya ties the name to 'it's alive', said on the rubbish heap.

carryVoice: Your line: the healer. To Jivaka, every plant could heal something. That's day seven hundred sixty-nine.
